title: Role-Based Access Control for AI Agents
summary: A role bounds the agent's tool access; the acting user's own permissions bound the request. A worked example of the two together, what ABAC and ReBAC cost instead, and the role-explosion symptoms to watch for.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**RBAC is the right place to start agent permissions and the wrong place to put everything, and the failure has had a name since 2014.**


NIST SP 800-162 calls it role explosion: trying to express situational decisions in roles "would require the creation of numerous roles that are ad hoc and limited in membership." The same document says RBAC "does not easily support multi-factor decisions" and that role assignments "tend to be based upon more static organizational positions."


The common reading is that this means moving to attributes. Sometimes it does. NIST is equally blunt in the other direction: the cost of ABAC "may exceed its benefits in the long term," and an ABAC system "may not lend itself well" to answering who has access to what before a request is made, which is the question auditors actually ask.


We are not arguing for a bigger role catalogue or against one. Roles are the reviewable ceiling. They were never the per-request decision, and for agents there are now two subjects to bound rather than one.


What to do today: keep roles verb-scoped and few, make an agent's effective permission the intersection of the agent's role and the acting user's own access, and route the record-level and requester-level questions to something built for them.
